extracted.intended_audience: Anglophone expatriate families (particularly American women/housewives) planning to live in Paris (early 20th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice and standards for living, finding, renting, and running a household in Paris (accommodation choices, leasing practice, utilities, taxes, insurance, child-rearing implications, shopping, and wartime considerations). Aimed at expatriates deciding how and where to live in Paris.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visit quartier foire for authentic Paris
rubrics_metrics.description: The little foire of each quarter (underwritten by shop-keepers and café proprietors) are never widely heralded; you stumble upon them by chance and they give the closest glimpse possible of Paris at play — spontaneous, improvised, and enjoyed by everybody.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend neighborhood fairs to see authentic Parisian life; expect merry-go-rounds, barkers, fortune-tellers, and inclusive participation. Anti-pattern: avoid if you dislike street-candy, novelty curiosities, or noisy popular amusements (the author warns readers who dislike such things to 'stay away from the foires').

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer June week-day excursions to avoid crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Most neighborhood foires are held in June; Sunday has drawbacks because the whole city is out and places are crowded, whereas on week-days there are no waits and plenty of room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan local excursions on June weekdays to avoid crowded trains and trams and to have more pleasant outings. Examples of accessible destinations by short train ride: Compiègne, Chantilly, Rambouillet, Versailles, Amiens, Chartres, Rheims, etc.; cheap luncheons and inexpensive cochers to visit ruins after lunch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation choice: hotel/pension vs keeping a home
rubrics_metrics.description: When in Paris without children, one can live in a hotel or a pension and possibly live as cheaply as in a home; but if making a protracted stay, many regret not having a home of their own, as 'you really cannot feel that you belong in Paris unless you are keeping house.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh short-term convenience of pensions (no lease, service provided) against long-term belonging and independence of a private home. For families (even with one baby), hotel/pension life quickly becomes unendurable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages and disadvantages of furnished rooms / pensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages: easy to find in desired quarter, no bother about service, no necessity to tie yourself up with a lease. Disadvantages: you get tired of the food, daily association with people you may not like, and (especially for women) no place to receive friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether short-term convenience outweighs loss of autonomy and social space; furnished apartments/pensions may look attractive but carry hidden costs and inconveniences (see inventory/charges guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow at least three months for apartment hunting and be proactive
rubrics_metrics.description: You always have three months at least in Paris to look for a home. It is not enough if you are undecided or lazy; it is plenty if you hunt with energy, persistence and enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time 'tramping the quarter' to find a suitable apartment; be decisive about desired amenities (e.g., two salons and three bedrooms, 'confort moderne' — central heat, electric light, baths, elevator) and act promptly when you find a good option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paris renting system: term leases and 3-6-9 standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Leases are by term (a term is three months) and can be canceled by giving one term's notice; most Paris leases are on a 3-6-9 year basis: you sign for three years, and if you do not give six months' notice before the end of the three-year term the lease continues for another equal period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that initial commitment can be short (three months) but standard practice uses multi-year contracts; failing to give required notice extends the lease. Knowledge of these conventions helps planning and negotiating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical lease clauses: tenant and proprietor obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Leases generally bind you to put furniture to the value of at least one year's rent, to live 'bourgeoisement' (carry on no business), to keep no dogs or other pets, and to sublet only with proprietor's consent. The proprietor agrees to provide proper concierge and elevator service, to heat the apartment from November 1 to March 31, and to furnish hot and cold water at fixed rates per cubic meter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect uniform clauses and verify them carefully; note the footnoted practical reality that 'no children' clauses are often enforced more than 'no dogs' language. These clauses are negotiable only within common Parisian practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventory (inventaire) and état des lieux: meticulous inspection and tenant liability
rubrics_metrics.description: French proprietors are meticulous; a furnished apartment comes with a detailed inventory recording objects and the state of walls, carpets, mattresses, etc. On leaving, agents find spots, cracks, nicks and charge the tenant. For unfurnished leases an architect may draw up an état des lieux which you must sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully negotiate and document the inventory/état des lieux on entry; expect to repaint, replace or clean items at termination if the agent disputes condition. Longer stays reduce the proportional burden of such incidental charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charges and fixed sums for building services
rubrics_metrics.description: Charges (your share towards carpets in halls, lighting, elevator, etc.) are in many leases represented by a fixed sum; where not fixed, you can often estimate them with reasonable certainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify whether charges are fixed or variable in the lease to avoid unexpected bills; inquire about typical amounts and what they cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxes and fiscal formalities associated with renting
rubrics_metrics.description: Municipal tax runs to about sixteen percent of the annual rental and now includes old taxes for windows and doors; there's also a small tax compensating the city for suppressed octroi. A new income tax exists; non-French subjects are not compelled to make a return of sources of income, but if taxed 'd'office' the collector may assess income as seven times the rental. The concierge is forbidden to allow you to move until you have shown receipts for the current year for all your taxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Budget for municipal taxes (~16% of annual rent) and learn local procedures; keep tax receipts current as moving out may be blocked without them. If uncertain about income-tax obligations, get advice about 'd'office' assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilities, fixtures, and telephones are tenant responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Proprietors furnish no chandeliers or other lights; you must buy fixtures and have them installed, sign contracts and make deposits for gas and electric light. The gas company will rent you a stove and a meter. Telephones are in the hands of the government: a direct telephone requires a contract and you pay for the instrument and installation; if you use the concierge's loge the telephone service is charged on your quarterly rent bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate additional one-time and recurring costs for lighting, heating hookups, and telephone installation; confirm who pays for what before moving in to avoid surprises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fire insurance and legal liability for neighbors and servants
rubrics_metrics.description: French law holds you responsible for damage to neighbors' apartments from water as well as fire if the fire starts in yours; your insurance policy insures your neighbors as well as yourself. French law also holds you liable for accidents to your servants — the servant need only prove the accident happened while working for you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain adequate fire (and related) insurance that covers third-party damage; understand employer liability for domestic servants and take appropriate precautions and insurance coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificat d'immatriculation required for foreigners' residence
rubrics_metrics.description: An old French police law requires all foreigners to secure a certificat d'immatriculation from the Prefecture of Police as the sine qua non to residence in Paris; before the war many ignored it, but wartime enforcement made it indispensable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure residency paperwork promptly to avoid administrative difficulties; do not rely on pre-war lax practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children and urban upbringing: tradeoffs and social attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: City childhood reportedly gives 'mental alertness, broad vision from infancy, self-reliance, [and] habits of industry' that country life may not, though theoretically the country is the best place to bring up children. Parisians (per author) often dislike children and you are more apt to be refused an apartment because you have children than because you have dogs or birds; 'NI CHIENS NI ENFANTS' signs frequently mean no children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor child-rearing priorities and potential social/housing discrimination when choosing between city and country living; understand local prejudice can affect housing availability for families.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servants: trade-offs and occasional maternal interlude
rubrics_metrics.description: Servants are described as a necessary evil for the housewife who wants to see something of the world, but an occasional interlude without a cook or nurse (when everything devolves on the mother) is good for both mother and children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance convenience of hired help against desire for closeness with children and self-reliance; plan occasional periods without servants for family bonding and personal oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market shopping vigilance and street purchasing techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Vegetables, fruits and nuts are mostly bought in open markets or from marchandes des quatre saisons; these sellers sometimes throw purchases on the scales and the buyer must be ready to steady the needle. Watch for inferior produce hidden beneath the top layer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When buying from street vendors, be alert to scales and display tricks; inspect goods carefully (look beneath layers) and be prepared to steady the scale to ensure accurate weight. Treat street-shopping as a lesson in bargaining and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical assessment of moving and living in wartime
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite fears, Paris in the early months of World War I functioned astonishingly normally: trains and moving-vans worked, freight arrived, labour was available, and food was abundant; panic and panic-driven exodus were not as widespread as some reports suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When considering whether to remain or return during a crisis, evaluate local conditions on the spot rather than relying solely on distant alarmist reports; practical considerations (family reunification, available services) may justify staying or returning.
